descriptor: Chinese state-controlled life insurer (A/H-share) · FY ends 31 December · reported in CNY · quoted in HKD

charts.title: Gross Profit, Operating Income & Net Income

sections.title: Insurance Operating Drivers
sections.subtitle: Embedded Value, VNB and solvency are the metrics that actually drive a life insurer's valuation -- GAAP revenue swings 20%+ a year on investment gains and is a weak proxy for the underlying book.

charts.title: Embedded Value
charts.annotation: H1 2026 EV of RMB1,614,207m is RMB57.11/share (HKD67.1); the quote trades at about 0.34x EV.

charts.title: Core Solvency Ratio
charts.annotation: Only recent periods disclose this under C-ROSS II; a sparse early history is expected, not a data gap.

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

gwp.title: Gross written premiums
gwp.content:
Gross written premiums (GWP) is the total premium income the insurer writes before reinsurance ceded, policy lapses or the IFRS 17 revenue-recognition adjustments. It is the cleanest read of new and renewal business volume.

For China Life: GWP grew 8.7% in FY2025 and 2.2% in H1 2026 -- far steadier than IFRS 17 "total revenues", which swung +81.5% in H1 2026 purely on investment gains. GWP, not revenue, is the line to read for underlying business growth.

What to watch:

  • GWP growth versus VNB growth -- rising volume at falling margin is a weaker outcome than the premium line alone suggests
  • First-year regular premium mix (bancassurance single-premium volumes are lower quality than agency regular premium)

embeddedValue.title: Embedded value
embeddedValue.content:
Embedded value (EV) is the actuarial measure of a life insurer's worth: adjusted net worth (shareholders' net assets at market value) plus the discounted value of in-force business, net of the cost of required capital. It is the insurance-industry equivalent of book value for a company whose liabilities are multi-decade policy obligations.

For China Life: H1 2026 EV of RMB1,614,207m is RMB57.11/share (HKD67.1 at the model fx rate); the H-share quote of HKD22.56 is about 0.34x EV, among the widest discounts in the sector and a direct reflection of the 43% structural A/H discount plus a payout ratio (16-17%) the market has not yet believed will rise.

What to watch:

  • EV growth (operating EV growth, not just the reported change, which includes investment variance)
  • Price/EV multiple relative to the company's own history and peers (1336.HK, 2378.HK)

vnb.title: Value of new business
vnb.content:
Value of new business (VNB) is the embedded value created by the policies sold in the period alone -- the actuarial profit margin on new sales, discounted for risk. It is the forward-looking growth engine behind the EV stock.

For China Life: VNB grew 35.7% in FY2025 and 33.7% in H1 2026 on the shift toward participating products and a 24.7% rise in first-year regular premiums -- the base case's main source of EV compounding, independent of the investment-return cycle that dominates reported net income.

What to watch:

  • VNB margin (VNB / first-year premium), not just the absolute figure -- margin mix shift can inflate VNB without better underlying economics
  • Whether VNB growth persists once the participating-product push matures

solvency.title: Core solvency ratio
solvency.content:
The core solvency ratio under China's C-ROSS II regime measures the highest-quality capital (core capital, chiefly retained earnings and share capital) against the regulatory capital requirement. It is the binding constraint on how much of earnings the insurer can pay out.

For China Life: core solvency moved from 128.8% to 156.8% in the six months to H1 2026, largely on OCI gains from the A-share rally -- the same market move that drove peak-cycle earnings. The base case's central bet, a payout ratio rising from 16% toward 45% by FY2035, depends on this buffer holding; a market reversal would cut solvency and cap the payout just as fast.

What to watch:

  • Solvency ratio direction versus equity-market moves -- it is not a steady operating metric
  • Distance above the regulatory floor (100% minimum, ~120% for an unconstrained payout in practice)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For China Life Insurance Company Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
